entries.title: Apple’s iPhone event will be packed with intrigue
entries.content:
[Macworld](https://www.macworld.com)

Apple always introduces its new iPhones and Apple Watches at a special event in September, and this year is no different.

Except this year, *everything* is different. The iPhones are different. The CEO is different. The event may be different. Here’s what we expect from Apple’s big September event.

## Time and Date

Apple always holds its events at 10 am PT, with iPhone launches usually taking place on the second Tuesday or Wednesday of September. This year, that is September 8 and 9.

Because Monday, September 7, is Labor Day in the United States, it’s likely that Apple will opt for Wednesday, the 9th, for its event, giving attendees the prior business day to travel. Otherwise, it could push it to the following week, likely Tuesday, September 15.

## The John Ternus show

Apple CEO [Tim Cook is going to retire](https://www.macworld.com/article/3119381/tim-cook-stepping-down-as-apple-ceo-in-shock-announcement.html) from the position on September 1, remaining on the company’s board of directors. He has named John Ternus, who was most recently senior vice president of hardware engineering, as his successor.

That means this is the first Apple Special Event in which Ternus will be the headliner, introducing the start of the event and thanking everyone at the end. Individual products are likely to be demonstrated by other Apple executives—they always are—but this is a big opportunity to shake up the format of Apple events in general.

Will we see a [return to live stage events](https://www.macworld.com/article/3206852/are-apples-live-events-returning-for-the-iphone-ultra-launch.html)? Will the structure and format of the pre-recorded video events change at all? Or will Ternus be essentially interchangeable for Tim Cook, with nothing else about these big product reveals changing at all? Will Apple make a “Turn” pun in its event invitation? We’ll have to wait and see.

## iPhone Ultra

For the first time in over a decade, Apple is going to dramatically change the iPhone’s form factor.

Apple is going to release a folding iPhone, which most are expecting to be called iPhone Ultra. It will fold in half like a book and be shaped sort of like a passport when closed; an unusual aspect ratio for any phone and especially an iPhone.

![Concept design of the back of the iPhone Fold closed and a separate image opened](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/iPhone-Fold-concept-3.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

This should be the relative size and shape of the folding iPhone Ultra.

Foundry

We expect two cameras (wide and ultrawide) on the back, one on the front, and the reintroduction of Touch ID in the side button for authentication. This is going to be a very premium product, with most rumors citing a starting price of $2,000 or more.

Not much is known about the software experience, though. Obviously, Apple will need to change some of how iOS looks and feels, and offer impressive new software features, to justify a folding phone with displays on the outside and inside and all new aspect ratios and sizes.

Check out our roundup of [rumors about the iPhone Ultra](https://www.macworld.com/article/2629813/iphone-ultra-folding-design-display-specs-release.html) for more.

## iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

The iPhone Ultra won’t be the only high-priced iPhone hitting the market this fall. With the standard iPhone 18 supposedly getting bumped back to a spring release, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are going to be the only other iPhones launched this fall.

We expect an upgraded [A20 Pro processor](https://www.macworld.com/article/3177014/apple-a20-pro-preview-cpu-gpu-performance-design-neural-engine-ai.html), a better modem (the C2 in many countries, possibly a Qualcomm modem in the U.S.), and a new [Dark Cherry signature color](https://www.macworld.com/article/3116701/iphone-18-pro-colors-revealed-exclusive-look-at-apples-2026-models.html).

![iPhone 18 Pro Cherry Red Mock Up ](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/New-iPhone-In-Cherry-Red.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

A dark red/cherry color should be the signature shade of the iPhone 18 Pro, along with Light Blue, Dark Gray, and Silver.

Foundry

For the most part, the iPhone 18 Pro will resemble the iPhone 17 Pro, but there should be a big upgrade to the rear camera (variable aperture, new sensor technology) and possibly a boost to 24 megapixels for the front camera. Battery capacity may go up by 6-8 percent, which could lead to longer battery life in conjunction with other improvements and optimizations.

Check out our roundup of [rumors about the iPhone 18 Pro](https://www.macworld.com/article/2953687/iphone-18-pro-2026-release-date-design-specs-rumors.html) for more.

## Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4

Apple always updates its Apple Watch line at the same time as the iPhone, whether it needs to or not.

That means that this year, we’ll see the [Apple Watch Series 12](https://www.macworld.com/article/3177024/apple-watch-series-12-2026-design-features-specs-release-date.html) and the Ultra 4. So far, none of the rumors suggest much of a change from the previous model. There will be a somewhat faster S12 processor, but major new health features or other changes don’t seem to be in the cards this year. Rumors say there [won’t be a new SE 4](https://www.macworld.com/article/3200021/dont-expect-a-new-apple-watch-se-this-fall.html) this year.

## Apple TV and Homepod mini

Both long overdue for an update, Apple has been waiting to release a new [Apple TV 4K](https://www.macworld.com/article/1373000/apple-tv-4k-3rd-generation-review.html) set-top box and the [HomePod mini](https://www.macworld.com/article/234895/homepod-mini-review.html) until it figured out how to really make the new Siri work.

Now, with a whole new Siri architecture coming in the OS 27 updates this fall, it’s finally ready to ship these products. Because Apple TV set-top boxes and HomePods act as a “home hub” for Apple’s smart home controls, Apple needed to make sure they’re capable of running the all-new Siri.

That said, we haven’t heard of any major new software features that make use of the improved hardware coming to Apple TV or HomePod. These new products will give you the new Siri experience just as a modern Apple Watch will, but the tvOS interface and features probably won’t get a big change. It’s more like: you’ll ask Siri something, and you’ll get Siri AI answers, not the old Siri.

![HomePod mini with siri activated](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/HomePod-mini.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

Foundry

## HomePad preview

The new Apple TV and HomePod mini will mark the start of a bigger, more ambitious smart home plan for Apple that all revolves around the new Siri and the expanded AI features that will be built out on top of it in the coming months and years. The main device we’re waiting for is the so-called [HomePad smart hub](https://www.macworld.com/article/3083918/homepad-reportedly-delayed-again-and-its-all-siris-fault-again.html) that has long been rumored.

The device is expected to have an iPad-like squarish screen that can either hang on a wall or dock to a speaker. It will reportedly run a new operating system dubbed HomeOS that is powered by Siri AI.

In his August 9 [Power On newsletter](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-08-09/apple-explores-apple-watch-shake-up-company-prepares-for-september-iphone-event), Mark Gurman reported that “a September preview of that product is plausible.” That could very well be Ternus’ surprise “One more Thing” to close the show. However, it is unlikely to go on sale until later in 2026 or early 2027.

entries.title: Insta360 launches X6, its flagship 360-degree 8K camera
entries.content:
![Two Insta360 devices on a bright background.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/024ZR1FCq5wv7UIczd0c2Hy/hero-image.png)

[Insta360](https://mashable.com/tech/insta360-hello-kitty-go-ultra-action-camera-sanrio) has launched the X6, its new flagship 8K 360 camera. Following [last year's X5](https://mashable.com/article/april-22-insta360-x5-camera-announced), the new X6 offers larger sensors, a higher frame rate, and 10-bit colour in an even more compact and rugged body.

The Insta360 X6 had been rumoured for a while, with an [FCC filing hinting at its release earlier this year](https://mashable.com/tech/insta360-x6-360-degree-camera-fcc-filings-launch-announcement-soon). The X5 was — and still is —  an impressive 360-degree camera, helping to cement Insta360 as a leader in the category upon its 2025 release. Now we finally know how Insta360 plans to improve upon it, with the X6 providing multiple upgrades.

SEE ALSO:
[Insta360 unveils cute Hello Kitty-themed action camera](https://mashable.com/tech/insta360-hello-kitty-go-ultra-action-camera-sanrio)

Firstly, the X6 boasts larger dual Sony 1/1.1-inch sensors as opposed to the X5's 1/1.28 sensors. This allows the X6 to take in more light, improving performance in dim environments and where there is significant contrast. Like the X5, the X6 has two dedicated imaging chips and one AI chip. However, the X6's AI chip has been upgraded from 5nm to 4nm, Insta360 stating that the camera has five times more computing power than its predecessor, while also having a reduced power draw.

![The Insta360 sitting in the snow.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/024ZR1FCq5wv7UIczd0c2Hy/images-2.fill.size_2000x1125.v1786532426.jpg)

Credit: Insta360

The Insta360 X6 can capture 360-degree footage at resolutions up to 8K at 50fps — up from the X5's maximum of 8K at 30fps. Its flat, traditional filming mode has also received a boost, reaching 5K at 60fps as opposed to the X5's maximum of 4K on the same frame rate. Photo mode now reaches 120MP for 360-degree images, or 42MP for flat pictures, compared to the X5's 72MP 360-degree and 18MP flat photos.

Another significant change is the X6's form factor. While it is slightly wider than the X5, measuring in at 50mm as opposed to 46 millimetres, its much shorter height more than makes up for this. The X6 reduces the X5's already fairly compact build by almost 25 millimetres, measuring approximately 100 millimetres tall. While nowhere near as small as [Insta360's GO action cameras](https://mashable.com/article/insta360-go-ultra-action-camera-specs-pricing), the X6 can easily fit in a jacket pocket.

![Two people looking at a Insta360 X6 camera on a selfie stick.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/024ZR1FCq5wv7UIczd0c2Hy/images-1.fill.size_2000x1125.v1786523881.jpg)

Credit: Insta360

This shorter build houses a 2.32-inch OLED touchscreen which can reach up to 1200 nits brightness, making it easier to preview footage in light environments. In addition to operating as a regular touchscreen, the X6's screen can also be used as a giant button for recording. This allows users to operate the camera even wearing thick gloves, or if you're struggling with the X6's typical controls.

The X6 further adds both 10-bit colour and Dolby Vision, features that aren't available in the X5. Alongside its ability to film in I-Log (Insta360's proprietary [log profile](https://www.cinematools.co/blog/why-you-should-be-filming-in-log-and-not-standard-profiles)), these shooting options enable the X6 to capture a wider dynamic range and more colours, providing a richer image and more flexibility when colour grading in post.

Insta360 states that the X6 can record 8K 30fps 360-degree video for up to 140 minutes on a single charge, surpassing the X5's runtime by 40 minutes. The X6 is also waterproof to 20 metres, an increase in depth of five metres, and has new replaceable lenses which the company claims are five-times more scratch-resistant (as well as more affordable). Mashable got to try replacing some X6 lenses, and found them not only simple to swap out, but also very satisfying.

The Insta360 X6 is available now, and comes in two colourways: Midnight Black and Arctic White. The Standard Version will set you back $699.99, and includes the X6 camera, a USB-C cable, a protective pouch, and a lens cloth. The $799.99 Essentials Bundle also includes these, but adds on an extra battery, invisible selfie stick, lens cap, fast charge case, and an extended warranty.

***Want more tech and digital culture news delivered to your inbox daily or sent straight to your device? Sign up for Mashable's [Top Stories newsletter](https://mashable.com/newsletters)*** ***or [get Mashable push alerts](https://mashable.com/life/how-to-set-up-mashable-push-notifications)*** ***today.***

entries.title: My favorite dating app just released *another* safety feature
entries.content:
![Pure's consent message on its My Media Rules feature.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01z9VcivZhSXSyGTReIfcFv/hero-image.png)

I love [Pure](https://zdcs.link/Qq4lo7?pageview_type=RSS&template=article&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Pure&object_type=article&object_uuid=01z9VcivZhSXSyGTReIfcFv&short_url=Qq4lo7&u=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Ffeeds%2Frss%2Fall "(opens in a new window)") for so many reasons. (It's particularly useful for anyone who's looking for no-fuss, hot AF phone sex.) But that level of sauciness isn't for everyone — and to be fair, Pure isn't the only place you'll find randos sending you unsolicited photos of their unruly trunks among the forest.

If you're a [Woman on the Internet](https://mashable.com/series/a-woman-on-the-internet) and you've used a [dating app](https://mashable.com/category/dating-relationships), you may have (unfortunately) received an unsolicited explicit photo, which is known as [cyberflashing](https://mashable.com/article/cyberflashing-unsolicited-dick-pics-terminology). According to the [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/02/02/the-experiences-of-u-s-online-daters/), about four in 10 online dating users (38 percent) report receiving a sexually explicit message or image they didn't ask for. For women ages 18 to 49, that number jumps to 56 percent.

So, Pure — one of the [most sex-positive dating apps I've ever tested](https://mashable.com/review/pure-dating-app-review) — is stepping up to stop cyberflashing with a brand-new feature called My Media Rules.

SEE ALSO:
[My favorite dating app just got even cooler with a new feed redesign](https://mashable.com/article/pure-dating-app-redesign-2026)

Developed directly from community feedback, My Media Rules takes the anxiety out of opening your messages. The tool lets you set your own universal boundaries for the app, meaning you can choose to auto-block all nude pics, turn off media sharing completely, or keep things open. You can even toggle these permissions on a chat-by-chat basis. Plus, if a graphic image appears for the first time, Pure prompts you to adjust your filters right then and there — and lets you decide whether you want to keep talking to the person who sent it.

![Pure's consent pop-up.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01z9VcivZhSXSyGTReIfcFv/images-2.fill.size_2000x1758.v1785379155.jpg)

No consent? No nude. Pure's built-in privacy tools blur sensitive content automatically.
Credit: Pure

"We love bringing fun and spontaneity to our community, but we believe that only works when it's backed by privacy, respect, and consent," Vicki Rool, Head of Trust & Safety at Pure, said in a statement. "People consistently told us they wanted more control over incoming media while keeping the spontaneity that makes Pure unique. We listened and built it. My Media Rules put that feedback into practice, giving people the choice of what type of media they receive."

This new feature adds to Pure's robust list of existing privacy tools, which includes native anti-screenshot protection, sensitive content blurring, and self-destructing photos and videos. (Which, honestly, is exactly why I recommend it for [sexting](https://mashable.com/roundup/best-sexting-apps-2026-tested)!)

entries.title: Two Bugs, One Setting: How DKA Silently Broke Our Fragments
entries.content:
![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*1lWKRdEiKb7JZIBGwlHPVg.png)

Every Android dev has seen the DKA checkbox in Developer Options. Almost nobody tests with it on. I didn’t either, until I had to track down two production bugs, months apart, that only reproduced with it on.

The first bug looked like a media picker that forgot how to respond to taps. The second looked like a profile screen that forgot how to navigate. Different features, different symptoms, different code paths. But the root cause was the same: state was initialized in a lifecycle callback that doesn’t fire when the fragment is recreated with a retained ViewModel.

This article is the story of both bugs. How they manifested, how I tracked them down, what the heap dump showed me, and the pattern that prevents an entire class of similar issues.

### A 30-Second Refresher on DKA + Retained ViewModels

When DKA is enabled and the user navigates away from your activity, the system destroys it. The fragment inside is destroyed too, but its **ViewModel survives** (held by ViewModelStore, which the framework retains across configuration changes and process recreation for the activity's task).

Here’s the critical part that’s easy to miss:

> When the activity is recreated, the fragment is re-instantiated, but its ViewModel is reused. Any initialization that happened inside a custom onCreate-style method tied to the ViewModel's lifecycle will NOT run again.

In our MVI architecture, we have a method called onCreateFeature(bundle, savedState). It's analogous to ViewModel.onCreate(). This is where the feature (our MVI engine), reducer, and all delegates are created. It runs exactly once: when the ViewModel is first created.

On fragment recreation with a retained ViewModel, onCreateFeature does not run. The fragment gets a fresh instance, but the feature is pulled from the surviving ViewModelStore. Everything you initialized in onCreateFeature? Still there, locked inside the old fragment instance that no longer exists.

One clarification, because it trips people up: DKA does not kill your process. It only destroys the Activity. Static fields, companion objects, anything living in your DI graph above Activity scope survives untouched. Real process death, the event onSaveInstanceState and SavedStateHandle exist for, is a different and more destructive case. DKA is actually the narrower problem: it only wipes state that lived inside the Activity or Fragment instance itself. That's exactly why ViewModelStore content, and anything a lazy delegate reads from it, is the only thing worth worrying about here.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*DzHjUOoGPyCGkCz1qyVlCg.png)

***Fig 1.*** *Fragment lifecycle with a retained ViewModel under DKA. The* *onCreateFeature callback fires only on first creation (left path). On recreation (right path), the ViewModel is reused from the surviving* *ViewModelStore, and* *onCreateFeature is skipped. Any* *lateinit fields it initialized remain unset.*

Let’s see what that looks like in practice.

### Bug #1: The Media Picker That Forgot Its Callbacks

### The Setup

Our media creation flow has a screen with a ViewPager2 containing a GalleryFragment (the system gallery picker) alongside tabs for drafts and templates. The host fragment creates the GalleryFragment lazily and sets up its callbacks:

<https://medium.com/media/7318b4d660089adbb48918ccb3b81333/href>

The galleryFragment is created via lazy, so it's instantiated on first access. The callbacks are set during that lazy initialization, once, on the first fragment instance.

### The Bug

With DKA enabled:

1. User opens the media creation screen. GalleryFragment is created, callbacks are set.
2. User navigates to the camera, which opens a new activity.
3. System destroys the host activity and the host fragment (but not the ViewPager2's internal state, which is saved and restored).
4. User returns. Activity is recreated, host fragment is re-instantiated.
5. ViewPager2's FragmentStateAdapter calls createFragment(), which creates a **new** GalleryFragment instance.
6. But galleryFragment (the lazy property) now holds the **old** instance, which is detached and dead. The callbacks were set on *that* instance.
7. The new GalleryFragment displayed on screen has no callbacks. Tapping photos does nothing. The camera button is dead.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*6GruEbn_wcCDW6Bn4jmRfg.png)

***Fig 2.*** *FragmentStateAdapter recreation under DKA. On first creation (top), the host fragment lazily creates* *GalleryFragment instance A and sets callbacks on it. On recreation (bottom), the adapter creates instance B, but the lazy property still points to the dead instance A. Instance B is displayed on screen with no callbacks attached. Instance A is retained in memory through the* *ViewModelStore GC root.*

No crash. No log. No error. The gallery renders fine: photos load, scrolling works. But nothing happens when you interact with it. The user is stuck on a screen that looks alive but isn’t.

### What the Memory Dump Reveals

This isn’t just a logic bug. It’s a hidden memory leak. The old GalleryFragment instance (instance A in Fig 2) is never garbage-collected. It's retained through a chain of references: the lazy property's Lazy wrapper holds a reference to the fragment, the fragment's callbacks capture the host fragment via lambda closures, and the host fragment's ViewModelStore keeps the entire chain alive.

When I profiled this with Android Studio Memory Profiler, the retention graph was unmistakable:

```
ViewModelStore  
  └─ MediaCreationFragment$ViewModel  
       └─ MediaCreationFragment (old instance, detached)  
            └─ Lazy<GalleryFragment> (galleryFragment property)  
                 └─ GalleryFragment (instance A - dead, detached)  
                      └─ View hierarchy (inflated but not attached)  
                           └─ ~2.3 MB of bitmaps and RecyclerView adapters
```

LeakCanary confirmed it with a heap dump. The old fragment held an entire detached View hierarchy: RecyclerViews, image views, bitmap caches, roughly 2.3 MB of retained memory that would never be freed. Every navigation away-and-back added another ghost fragment to this chain. After 5 round-trips, the app was holding ~11 MB of dead UI trees.

**Methodology:** Measured on a Pixel 6 running API 34. Reproduced by manually navigating to the camera and back 5 times with DKA enabled. Heap dumps captured via Android Studio Memory Profiler “Capture heap dump” button after each round-trip. LeakCanary (version 2.14) automatically triggered on the 2nd round-trip. Retained size confirmed via “Show nearest GC root” in the profiler’s retained objects view.

This is the silent danger of caching Fragment instances: they drag their entire View hierarchy with them, and the ViewModelStore acts as a GC root that prevents collection.

### The Discovery

QA reported this with a vague “gallery doesn’t work after coming back from camera.” My first instinct was to blame the camera. Maybe it was consuming some shared resource, holding a lock, or corrupting state. I spent a day chasing that hypothesis before realizing the camera worked fine. It was the gallery that was broken on return.

The breakthrough came when I enabled DKA on my own device and reproduced it consistently. The key observation: the gallery fragment instance visible on screen was not the same object as the one we had configured. The FragmentStateAdapter had recreated it, and our lazy property was pointing at a ghost. The memory profiler confirmed this by showing two GalleryFragment instances, only one of which was attached.

The answer was in the FragmentStateAdapter documentation all along: createFragment() is called every time the adapter needs a fragment instance. The original code treated it like a one-time factory, but it's a recurring factory.

### The Fix

The core insight: don’t store the fragment instance at all. Store the *data needed to configure it*, and apply that data every time the fragment is (re)created.

I extracted all callbacks into a plain data holder:

<https://medium.com/media/5d4a20d5b7f17e5f47aaa65254e52c7a/href>

The FragmentStateAdapter now creates a fresh GalleryFragment on every createFragment() call, and the host fragment re-applies callbacks in onViewCreated:

<https://medium.com/media/dd97162f2a8ff46297978ab56230e100/href>

Instead of caching the fragment instance, we look it up from childFragmentManager every time. The GalleryFragmentData is safe to hold because it's just a data class with lambda references, all of which capture the host fragment (which survives as long as the childFragmentManager is alive).

After this fix, the memory leak disappeared. With no cached fragment instance, there’s no GC root holding dead View hierarchies. LeakCanary reported zero leaks across 20 round-trip navigation cycles.

There was also a secondary issue. A DialogFragment for audio editing crashed on DKA restoration because it needed camera API access through a delegate that wasn't available after recreation. The fix there was blunt but effective:

<https://medium.com/media/efc1ce2340bafd374a0d76a79d27186b/href>

Not elegant, but correct. If savedInstanceState != null, we're being restored after DKA, and the dialog can't function. Better to dismiss cleanly than to crash.

### Bug #2: The Profile That Forgot How to Navigate

### The Setup

This one appeared months later, in a completely different part of the app. Our profile screen uses an MVI architecture where the fragment hosts a Feature (the MVI engine) and a SideEffectDelegate that handles navigation commands emitted by the feature.

The delegate was initialized in onCreateFeature, our equivalent of ViewModel.onCreate():

<https://medium.com/media/81e8c81b585f722c6bde442864684de1/href>

See that guard: if (::sideEffectDelegate.isInitialized)? Someone added that as a safety net without understanding why. It acknowledged that the delegate *might* not be initialized when render was called, but never stopped to ask why a field initialized in onCreateFeature wouldn't be ready by the time render ran. The answer, of course, was DKA.

### The Bug

With DKA enabled:

1. User opens a profile. onCreateFeature runs, delegate is created, everything works.
2. User switches to another app.
3. System destroys the activity and fragment. The ViewModelStore survives. The ProfileFeature and its reducer are retained.
4. User returns. Activity is recreated, fragment is re-instantiated.
5. onCreateFeature does not run. The feature already exists in the retained ViewModelStore.
6. sideEffectDelegate is lateinit and was never assigned. It's uninitialized.
7. The feature’s sideEffectChannel starts emitting navigation commands, but ::sideEffectDelegate.isInitialized returns false, so every navigation command is silently swallowed.

The user sees the profile render correctly (because render works; it reads from the feature's state, which survived). But they can't tap anything that requires navigation. Tapping a wall post does nothing. Tapping a photo does nothing. Switching tabs updates the UI, but the currentTab field resets to the default because that was also initialized in onCreateFeature.

The whole screen renders but doesn’t navigate. Users see a frozen profile that looks correct but responds to nothing.

### The Same Pattern, Hiding in Three More Places

Once I identified the root cause, I grepped the file for every field initialized in onCreateFeature. I found the same bug hiding in three more places:

<https://medium.com/media/77a76e599f96b9d1fe409e5126e5cd2e/href>

currentTab was set to reducer.unsafeState().selectedTab in onCreateFeature. On restoration, it stayed at Wall(), the default, even if the user was on the Photos tab.

isFromEditor was set from params.isFromEditor in onCreateFeature. On restoration, it was false, so editor-specific behavior was silently skipped.

clickTracker was a local variable inside onCreateFeature, passed to the navigator. On restoration, a new tracker was created separately, splitting analytics. Two trackers for the same screen, neither consistent.

### The Fix

Every field that was previously initialized in onCreateFeature became lazy:

<https://medium.com/media/bd1ddceb72f699735facee439ac8e39a/href>

The key change for currentTab: instead of reading the initial value from the reducer in onCreateFeature, it reads from the feature's live state on first access. If onCreateFeature didn't run, the feature still exists (retained), and its state still holds the correct selected tab.

The render method was simplified. No more isInitialized guard:

<https://medium.com/media/73209807a4cf3efb01a8ed163a7488b7/href>

And onDestroy was updated to guard against accessing uninitialized lazy values:

<https://medium.com/media/e4822c10f8bdb4984750d61427808817/href>

There was one more subtlety. autoJoinSignature controlled whether the app auto-joined a community when opening it via a deep link. It was previously read from params inside onCreateFeature (which had access to savedState). On DKA restoration, onCreateFeature doesn't run, so the signature stays null. That's actually correct: the auto-join should only happen on the first open, not on recreation.

<https://medium.com/media/e20ecf7aba5f0128797a218c4250a2a8/href>

Sometimes the absence of initialization is the right behavior. You just need to be explicit about it.

### The Pattern

Both bugs share the same shape:

```
Something is initialized in a lifecycle callback that runs ONCE  
(ViewModel creation). On fragment recreation with retained VM,  
that callback doesn't fire. The something stays uninitialized.  
Nothing crashes. It just doesn't work.
```

The fix in both cases was the same: move initialization to lazy so it runs on first access, whenever that happens. First creation or tenth recreation, doesn't matter.

![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*lj85bUtPSSFPv74Ut9Ki4A.png)

***Fig 3.****lateinit vs* *lazy comparison. The last row is the key insight:* *lateinit breaks silently when the init callback is skipped on DKA recreation, while* *lazy always runs on first access.*

If you’re using lateinit in a Fragment and initializing it in onCreate, onCreateView, or a ViewModel-style onCreate method, ask yourself: will this run again if the fragment is recreated with a retained ViewModel? If the answer is no, use lazy.

One more detail worth tightening: every lazy { } in this article defaults to LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED, which takes a lock on first access to guard against two threads racing to initialize the value. Fragments live on the main thread. Nothing in galleryFragment, sideEffectDelegate, or isFromEditor is ever touched from a background thread, so that lock buys nothing but a few wasted cycles on every access. Declare them as lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { ... } instead. It won't fix a bug, but it's the kind of detail that separates code that happens to work from code that's actually correct for the thread model it runs in.

### The DKA Checklist

Before shipping a fragment with retained ViewModels, check every field initialized in lifecycle callbacks:

1. **Is it** **lateinit?** If yes, verify the init callback fires on recreation. If not, switch to lazy.
2. **Is it a** **var with a default value?** If yes, verify the default is correct on recreation. If not, make it lazy and read from surviving state.
3. **Are you storing a Fragment instance reference?** The reference may point to a dead fragment after recreation. Look it up from FragmentManager instead.
4. **Are callbacks set on a Fragment instance?** Re-apply them in onViewCreated, every time.
5. **Is there an****::field.isInitialized guard?** That's a smell. It means you know the field might not be initialized, but you're working around it instead of fixing the root cause.

### How to Catch These Bugs Automatically

The checklist is good for manual review, but the real defense is automation. Here are three complementary approaches.

### 1. Instrumentation Test with ActivityScenario.recreate()

The most direct way to verify your fragment survives recreation is to recreate it in a test:

<https://medium.com/media/500fb1b3e8d25db5096c166371dad348/href>

The key line is scenario.recreate(). This does exactly what DKA does: destroys the activity, recreates it, and reuses the ViewModelStore. If your fragment has a lateinit field that's only initialized in a ViewModel-style onCreate, this test will fail on the assertion.

The test catches both bugs from this article. Bug #1 (callbacks lost) would fail because the gallery fragment’s callbacks are gone. Bug #2 (navigation lost) would fail because sideEffectDelegate is uninitialized.

### 2. Enable DKA in Debug Builds

You can’t force DKA programmatically (it’s a system setting that requires WRITE\_SECURE\_SETTINGS), but you can make it a team habit. Tell everyone to enable DKA in Developer Options and never turn it off. Make it part of onboarding. If QA enables it too, you'll catch these bugs before they reach production.

### 3. LeakCanary in Debug Builds

Add LeakCanary to your debug build to catch retained fragment instances automatically:

<https://medium.com/media/d968c5efa1b8997374ff9edafca60ca8/href>

No configuration needed. LeakCanary dumps the heap when it detects a retained fragment and shows you the exact retention chain. The 2.3 MB leak from Bug #1 was found manually via Memory Profiler, but LeakCanary would have caught it automatically starting from the 2nd round-trip.

### Why This Is Hard to Catch

DKA bugs are invisible in normal development because:

* They don’t crash. The code compiles, runs, and produces no errors. The feature just stops working in one specific scenario.
* They look like other bugs. “Navigation doesn’t work” could be a routing bug, a state bug, a UI bug, anything. The connection to a recreated ViewModel is not obvious.
* They leak memory silently. As shown in the memory forensics section, cached fragment instances create retention chains through ViewModelStore that are only visible under heap analysis, not in normal logs or crash reports.

### Beyond Our MVI Stack

This pattern is not specific to our MVI framework. The same bug class appears anywhere a long-lived component outlives the short-lived view layer that configures it.

**Jetpack MVVM (ViewModel + StateFlow):** If you initialize a lateinit navigation controller or analytics tracker inside ViewModel.init and reference it from a Fragment, you have the same problem. The ViewModel survives recreation; the Fragment doesn't. SavedStateHandle helps with data, but not with delegate/callback initialization.

**MVIKotlin / Orbit / Redux-style stores:** Same shape. The store survives, the view is recreated. Anything the view configured on the store (observers, callbacks, bootstrappers) needs to be re-applied on every view creation, not just the first.

**Non-Android actor/service patterns:** A long-lived service actor that receives configuration from a short-lived client. If the client is replaced and the configuration was one-time, the actor keeps running with stale or missing configuration.

The general principle: **never bind critical state initialization to a lifecycle callback that may be skipped during component recreation.** Use lazy initialization with fallback to surviving state. It’s not an Android-specific insight. It’s a property of any system with asymmetric component lifetimes.

### Conclusion

Two bugs. Two different features. Two different symptoms. One root cause: initializing state in a lifecycle callback that doesn’t fire on fragment recreation with a retained ViewModel.

The fix was the same both times: lazy initialization. Lazy defers initialization to the moment of first use, whenever that is, instead of tying it to a specific lifecycle callback that may or may not run.

After fixing these two bugs, I audited the codebase for similar patterns and found five more instances of lateinit fields initialized in onCreateFeature. All had the same potential for silent breakage on DKA. Each took about ten minutes to convert to lazy once the pattern was clear.

If you take one thing from this article: enable DKA right now, open your most complex screen, and navigate away and back. You might be surprised by what’s silently broken.

![](https://medium.com/_/stat?event=post.clientViewed&referrerSource=full_rss&postId=de9567449e6c)

---

[Two Bugs, One Setting: How DKA Silently Broke Our Fragments](https://proandroiddev.com/two-bugs-one-setting-how-dka-silently-broke-our-fragments-de9567449e6c) was originally published in [ProAndroidDev](https://proandroiddev.com) on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

entries.title: Wilkie escalates gambling reform fight with anti-corruption referral targeting Labor government
entries.content:
![Andrew Wilkie and gambling reform advocates at Parliament House calling for stronger gambling advertising restrictions and harm-reduction reforms.](https://readwrite.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Wilkie-escalates-gambling-reform-fight-with-anti-corruption-referral-targeting-Labor-government-300x200.png)

Independent MP Andrew Wilkie has taken the fight over gambling reform to the National Anti-Corruption Commission, asking it to examine whether industry influence improperly shaped federal government policy.

> Today I have referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission my concern that individuals in the Federal Government, when formulating gambling policy, have been improperly influenced by individuals in the private sector. [#auspol](https://x.com/hashtag/auspol?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) [#politas](https://x.com/hashtag/politas?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) [pic.twitter.com/Phf9CVJJos](https://t.co/Phf9CVJJos)
>
> — Andrew Wilkie MP (@WilkieMP) [August 12, 2026](https://x.com/WilkieMP/status/2087340038694842587?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

In a letter dated Wednesday (August 12), Wilkie said he was concerned “individuals in the Federal Government, when formulating gambling reform policy, have been improperly influenced by individuals in the private sector, most obviously but not exclusively through donations, gifts, hospitality and personal relationships.”

He argued the policy that emerged was “so clearly at odds with research, public opinion and the public interest” that putting it into effect “could be characterised, in my opinion, as serious corruption in the Commonwealth public sector.”

> [pic.twitter.com/wOCxA4oQQJ](https://t.co/wOCxA4oQQJ)
>
> — Andrew Wilkie MP (@WilkieMP) [August 12, 2026](https://x.com/WilkieMP/status/2087387512776138815?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The independent MP pointed to reporting published by [The Sydney Morning Herald](https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/labor-s-millions-in-gambling-donations-revealed-amid-last-ditch-push-for-reform-20260714-p60f59.html) and The Age on July 22. He said the reports, if accurate, raised questions about whether private interests had affected how public officials exercised their powers and whether officials had breached public trust.

Wilkie made clear that accepting political donations, lobbying governments and making policy decisions are all legal. He was also “not making any allegation against any specific individual” in asking the commission to look more broadly at what happened.

Even so, he said the government’s conduct had gone beyond “all reasonable limits,” adding: “If this doesn’t ‘cross the line’, then I dread to think what would.”

## Wilkie points to industry donations as questions raised over gambling policy influence

After making the referral, Wilkie said political support had to have boundaries.

“There must be a point at which support for a party or candidate becomes buying a party or a candidate.”

Using Australian Electoral Commission donor disclosures, Wilkie said gambling companies gave about $5 million to Labor across the 2020-21 to 2024-25 financial years. He put Liberal Party donations from the industry at between $4 million and $5 million over the same period.

His criticism has sharpened in recent weeks. Earlier this month, Wilkie accused Labor of walking away from meaningful reform after taking millions of dollars from gambling businesses.

He also attacked the Tasmanian Treasurer over the reversal of poker machine closing-hour changes, saying the decision returned the state to outdated harm-reduction settings. He said the Treasurer had “sold his soul to the gambling industry.”

Labor is facing pressure from the Coalition as well. During parliamentary debate, Liberal MP Simon Kennedy said the government had been pushed into negotiations after previously maintaining its bill would not change.

> Labor voted against the inquiry that exposed the problems with its own gambling laws. Now those failures have to be fixed. [pic.twitter.com/EXPNNrR6Ha](https://t.co/EXPNNrR6Ha)
>
> — Simon Kennedy MP (@SimonKennedyMP) [August 11, 2026](https://x.com/SimonKennedyMP/status/2087043344140571134?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

“The Prime Minister has lost the public debate on [gambling advertising](https://readwrite.com/australia-gambling-ads-critics-say-reforms-fall-short/),” Kennedy said.

Kennedy said a Senate inquiry had highlighted two serious gaps. In his view, Labor had not dealt strongly enough with gambling inducements and had left online advertising largely unrestricted, including digital advertising connected with live sport.

During his account of evidence presented to the inquiry, Kennedy told Parliament: “We heard about cocaine, we heard about prostitutes.”

He said Coalition senators Sarah Henderson and Angus Taylor were working on tougher amendments and called for an independent review after the next federal election.

## Senate evidence pushes Labor toward tougher gambling restrictions

The inquiry attracted particular attention after allegations emerged about how some high-value gamblers were treated by VIP account managers.

Former NRL player Luke Bateman, who has publicly discussed losing about $1 million through gambling addiction, told senators he had been offered alcohol, illicit drugs and other inducements while being encouraged to keep betting.

> David Pocock left stunned as Luke Bateman who has recovered from a serious gambling addiction also reveals he was being offered drugs,  
> Pocock “The actual leaders of these companies knew what was happening?”  
> Bateman “Not only did they know, they were participating in it.”![💥](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f4a5.png) [pic.twitter.com/6aA6ktAQlz](https://t.co/6aA6ktAQlz)
>
> — stranger (@strangerous10) [August 3, 2026](https://x.com/strangerous10/status/2084097349899718689?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Gambling reform campaigner Tim Costello said people he had supported had described similar experiences. He argued the accounts showed how inducements could be used to keep vulnerable customers gambling.

Sportsbet and Tabcorp rejected the allegations. Both told the inquiry they had no evidence that such behavior was part of their operations and said allegations of criminal conduct should go to police.

The testimony created another problem for Labor because its legislation did not adopt a central recommendation from the [late Peta Murphy’s parliamentary inquiry](https://readwrite.com/australia-has-a-gambling-addiction-write-former-prime-ministers/): immediately banning online gambling inducements and advertising for those inducements.

After the hearings, the government indicated it was willing to negotiate tougher inducement restrictions with the Coalition to get its legislation through Parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese later told Labor’s caucus that further measures would target inducements and children’s exposure to gambling advertising.

> NEWS: We’re cutting gambling ads on TV, radio, online and on the field.
>
> — Anthony Albanese (@AlboMP) [April 2, 2026](https://x.com/AlboMP/status/2039521653181534653?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Albanese has characterized the package as Australia’s strongest anti-gambling legislation. Taylor has described negotiations as constructive, but independents and public health campaigners say the changes remain well short of Murphy’s recommendations.

Children’s exposure also became a flashpoint during the Senate hearings. Henderson questioned Australian Communications and Media Authority executive manager Rochelle Zurnamer about existing restrictions on gambling advertisements around children’s programs.

> Labor’s gambling reform bill is riddled with deficiencies and must be significantly amended, further evidence of Anika Wells’ incompetence and the government’s failure to take gambling harm seriously.   
>   
> Questioning the regulator, the Australian Communications and Media Authority,… [pic.twitter.com/I4pKcLQLAu](https://t.co/I4pKcLQLAu)
>
> — Senator Sarah Henderson (@SenSHenderson) [August 4, 2026](https://x.com/SenSHenderson/status/2084595690098094270?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Zurnamer explained those protections currently sit in the Commercial Television Code of Practice rather than legislation. She said ACMA expected them to remain, despite the new bill not addressing the matter.

Henderson said that was not enough.

“The current prohibition on running gambling ads during children’s, pre-school and general classified programming, or programming targeted to children, is not in this bill,” she said. “I would put to you that that is outrageous.”

## Labor’s compromise leaves campaigners demanding a full advertising ban

Labor’s planned rules, due to begin on 1 January 2027, [would restrict gambling advertising](https://readwrite.com/australia-government-slammed-for-u-turn-on-gambling-ad-ban/) without imposing a complete ban. Television advertising would be capped, radio ads restricted during school commuting periods and advertising barred during live sports broadcasts.

The package would also bring digital platforms under new rules using age verification and opt-out systems. Celebrity endorsements would be banned, while betting promotions would disappear from stadiums and player uniforms.

Albanese says the approach is designed to reduce children’s exposure while keeping legal gambling available to adults. Communications Minister Anika Wells has framed the reforms as a way of weakening the link between sport and gambling.

Critics see a compromise that retreats from calls for a comprehensive advertising ban.

The government’s impact analysis says Australians lose more than $32 billion to gambling each year and estimates the wider annual social cost of wagering harm at $26.8 billion. It identifies advertising as an important force in normalizing gambling, particularly for younger people.

But the analysis also says a total advertising ban would carry substantial financial consequences for broadcasters, sporting bodies and media companies. Labor instead chose a model expected to cut wagering activity by about 0.8 per cent and deliver an estimated $107.1 million in annual net public benefit from reduced harm.

The Alliance for Gambling Reform says the government has [waited too long to implement the Murphy inquiry’s 31 recommendations](https://readwrite.com/alliance-australia-gambling-ads-reform-youth-harm/), including a national regulator and comprehensive advertising ban. Campaigners point to research suggesting about 600,000 Australians under 18 already gamble, spending roughly $18 million a year.

Crossbench MPs are also demanding stronger action. Independent MP Helen Haines has called Labor’s legislation “unconscionable,” while proposing tighter advertising restrictions, a national regulator and public reporting of harm indicators by gambling companies.

[Senator David Pocock has called Labor’s approach](https://readwrite.com/senator-david-pocock-ousted-sports-club-gambling-sponsorship-row/) “a tragedy,” arguing it falls short of public support for tougher controls.

Wilkie’s NACC referral now takes the dispute beyond arguments about what the legislation should contain. It asks whether the process behind the government’s policy warrants scrutiny too.

The commission does not have to investigate every referral, and Wilkie has stopped short of accusing any named person of criminal wrongdoing. But his intervention ensures questions about donations, lobbying, hospitality and relationships.

*Featured image: Andrew Wilkie MP via X*

The post [Wilkie escalates gambling reform fight with anti-corruption referral targeting Labor government](https://readwrite.com/wilkie-gambling-reform-anti-corruption-referral-labor/) appeared first on [ReadWrite](https://readwrite.com).

entries.title: FlightAware drops federal lawsuit against Kalshi after seeking emergency court relief
entries.content:
![Kalshi logo over a flight departures board showing multiple cancelled flights after FlightAware dropped its federal trademark lawsuit over flight cancellation prediction markets.](https://readwrite.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FlightAware-ends-Kalshi-federal-lawsuit-without-prejudice-300x200.png)

FlightAware has voluntarily dismissed its federal lawsuit against prediction market operator Kalshi [just one day after filing the case](https://readwrite.com/flightaware-sues-kalshi-flight-cancellation-betting-trademark/), bringing the litigation to an abrupt halt while preserving its ability to sue again in the future.

The [notice of voluntary dismissal](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.670254/gov.uscourts.nysd.670254.15.0.pdf) was filed August 11 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. FlightAware ended the case without prejudice under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i), a rule that allows plaintiffs to withdraw an action before defendants file an answer or motion for summary judgment.

The dismissal applies to every defendant named in the lawsuit: Kalshi Inc., KalshiEX LLC, Kalshi Klear Inc. and Kalshi Klear LLC. The filing does not explain why FlightAware chose to withdraw the case and makes no reference to any settlement or agreement between the parties.

The lawsuit had been filed only a day earlier and sought emergency relief over Kalshi’s flight cancellation prediction markets.

## FlightAware leaves the door open to sue Kalshi again

In its complaint, FlightAware accused Kalshi of using its flight-tracking data and trademarks without authorization to operate and settle contracts allowing users to wager on airline cancellations. The company sought damages and an injunction to stop Kalshi from using its information and branding.

According to the complaint, Kalshi identified FlightAware as the “Primary Source Agency” for its aviation markets, displayed the FlightAware trademark, linked users to the company’s website and stated that market outcomes were “verified from FlightAware.” FlightAware argued those references created the false impression that it endorsed or participated in the betting products.

The complaint also alleged Kalshi had agreed not to use FlightAware’s AeroAPI data for commercial purposes, including gambling or prediction markets, but continued doing so after receiving a cease-and-desist letter. FlightAware said Kalshi rejected those claims, arguing its references constituted nominative fair use before later adding disclaimers denying any endorsement.

FlightAware further claimed mistaken assumptions that it supported the markets harmed its reputation for independence and said it has “never operated, sponsored, promoted, or participated in a market that permits customers to wager on whether flights will be delayed or cancelled.”

> FlightAware just VOLUNTARILY DISMISSED its entire lawsuit against Kalshi.  
>   
> Again, filed yesterday seeking emergency relief over the flight-cancellation betting markets.  
>   
> Dismissed today under Rule 41(a)(1)(A)(i) (without prejudice) before Kalshi even answered.  
>   
> When a plaintiff… <https://t.co/7M3dFhldvz> [pic.twitter.com/EnL0qdgEAA](https://t.co/EnL0qdgEAA)
>
> — Ariel Givner (@GivnerAriel) [August 12, 2026](https://x.com/GivnerAriel/status/2087334461025259845?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Commentators noted the unusual timing of the dismissal. Ariel Givner, posting on X, wrote that FlightAware had voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit before Kalshi filed any response, adding that cases dropped so quickly after requesting a temporary restraining order often suggest the parties may have reached a private resolution. Neither FlightAware nor Kalshi has publicly confirmed any agreement.

Because the dismissal was entered without prejudice, the company remains free to bring similar claims again if it chooses.

*Featured image: Kalshi / Canva*

The post [FlightAware drops federal lawsuit against Kalshi after seeking emergency court relief](https://readwrite.com/flightaware-drops-federal-lawsuit-against-kalshi/) appeared first on [ReadWrite](https://readwrite.com).

entries.title: CFTC steps in to shield Kalshi from New York shutdown attempt
entries.content:
![Kalshi logo beside the New York City skyline as the CFTC intervenes in the legal dispute over the prediction market platform.](https://readwrite.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/CFTC-steps-in-to-shield-Kalshi-from-New-York-shutdown-attempt-300x200.png)

Kalshi can keep operating for now after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) invoked its emergency powers, warning that an effort by New York to restrict the prediction-market exchange could disrupt derivatives markets in the United States and internationally if the platform were forced to shut down.

The [CFTC issued its emergency order](https://www.cftc.gov/media/14471/OGC_MarketEmergencyDeclarationOrder081126/download) on August 11 after Kalshi notified the regulator on August 1 that New York’s pending request for a temporary restraining order had created what it described as an imminent market emergency. The order directs Kalshi to continue operating under its normal business practices and the Core Principles of the Commodity Exchange Act while the legal dispute continues.

> This is the first time the CFTC has exercised its emergency authority in over three weeks. <https://t.co/iRaz00Ttdo>
>
> — Rob Schwartz (@FormerCFTCGC) [August 11, 2026](https://x.com/FormerCFTCGC/status/2087314649838399493?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The latest development comes less than two weeks after [New York Attorney General Letitia James filed a lawsuit alleging Kalshi](https://readwrite.com/new-york-sues-kalshi-alleging-illegal-prediction-markets-state-gambling-laws/) is operating an illegal gambling business by offering contracts tied to sports, elections, culture and other future events without a New York gaming license. The lawsuit seeks a permanent injunction blocking the company from operating in the state, along with restitution, disgorgement of alleged profits, civil penalties and a full accounting of customer activity.

In its request for emergency relief, New York also sought a temporary restraining order preventing Kalshi from offering contracts involving sports, culture, elections and “other events” within or from New York or to people in the state.

According to the CFTC, that wording is so wide-ranging that it would effectively prohibit Kalshi from listing any event contracts because the state did not define or limit what qualifies as “other events.” The regulator also pointed out that New York is seeking Kalshi’s profits from event contracts, a penalty equal to three times those profits and at least $36 billion in compensatory damages, excluding punitive damages and costs. The order also points out that New York’s verified petition referenced Kalshi’s publicly reported $22 billion valuation.

## CFTC argues lawsuit risks consequences beyond the prediction market

The commission’s 10-page order lays out why it believes immediate intervention was necessary, arguing that a sudden shutdown would harm Kalshi, its customers and the agency’s authority to regulate federally designated derivatives exchanges.

> New York intends to make event contract derivatives waste away under its iron curtain of state gaming laws before the courts issue final rulings. The [@CFTC](https://x.com/CFTC?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) is required by law to ensure order in the derivatives markets, and that is what we’ve done today.   
>   
> Read more:…
>
> — Mike Selig (@ChairmanSelig) [August 11, 2026](https://x.com/ChairmanSelig/status/2087282004307923101?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

“Put simply, New York’s lawsuit threatens to prevent a CFTC-registered DCM from offering event contracts to anyone in the world,” the commission said in its order. “That unprecedented assertion of state authority cuts at the very heart of the Commission’s jurisdiction and would have significant adverse ramifications for national and international financial markets.”

The CFTC said Kalshi’s contracts are used to hedge or speculate on events ranging from Federal Reserve interest-rate decisions and cryptocurrency prices to drought conditions, recession risks and shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Removing access to those contracts, the agency said, could alter the financial risk profiles of market participants across the United States and abroad.

The regulator also warned that an abrupt halt could distort pricing as traders rapidly shift positions to competing exchanges, creating unusual trading activity unrelated to the underlying events. It added that markets could begin pricing in the possibility that individual states could shut down federally regulated exchanges.

Another concern raised by the commission involves forced liquidation. The order describes an arbitrage trader holding a Kalshi position alongside an offsetting position on another platform. If the Kalshi position had to be liquidated unexpectedly, the trader could be left with a one-sided exposure.

“As a result of dynamics of this variety, there may be significant price volatility in derivatives markets and other markets, threatening systemic harm,” the commission said.

CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig separately criticized New York’s legal strategy.

“New York intends to make event contract derivatives waste away under its iron curtain of state gaming laws before the courts get the chance to issue final rulings,” [said Chairman Michael S. Selig](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/9281-26). “Congress did not intend for derivatives exchanges to be regulated under a patchwork of state gaming laws. These are financial exchanges that offer financial instruments and operate across state lines.

“They match the bid from a resident of one state with the offer of a resident from another state and submit the trade to a clearinghouse that backstops the transactions of customers throughout the country. New York has no business regulating these interstate financial markets. The Commission is required by law to ensure order in these markets, and that is what we have done today.”

## New York escalates pressure on Kalshi

On August 6, state investigators with the New York State Gaming Commission issued document subpoenas to Kalshi Inc. and KalshiEX LLC seeking records related to sports-event contracts, including transactions involving people under the age of 21. According to legal analyst Daniel Wallach, the [subpoenas are limited to sports contracts](https://readwrite.com/new-york-subpoenas-kalshi-sports-contracts/) and represent the first known government subpoena directed at Kalshi.

Wallach said the requests seek records concerning Kalshi’s sports offerings, corporate structure and ownership, and suggested they help explain why the company quickly removed New York’s lawsuit to federal court after it was filed on July 31.

> You tried to make the same argument in the SDNY on an emergency basis, and Judge Rakoff denied your motion for a TRO to block NY from enforcing its gaming laws in state court. That’s 3 rulings from NY and 1 in CT—all federal. They saw you in court and beat you on your own turf. <https://t.co/YQSUbTPcmL>
>
> — Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) [August 11, 2026](https://x.com/WALLACHLEGAL/status/2087319165514260716?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The subpoenas require Kalshi to produce the requested records by August 14 as the Gaming Commission continues its investigation.

New York maintains that Kalshi’s products are gambling rather than federally protected financial derivatives and argues the company has ignored state gaming laws despite earlier enforcement efforts, including a cease-and-desist order issued in 2025.

Kalshi removed the case to federal court on the same day the lawsuit was filed. A New York judge later ruled the state’s request for [immediate injunctive relief was moot](https://readwrite.com/new-york-kalshi-case-federal-removal/) because of the removal, leaving the federal court to determine the next steps while the Gaming Commission’s separate investigation continues.

The CFTC’s August 11 emergency order remains in effect while the litigation proceeds and directs Kalshi to continue performing its exchange functions under its normal practices and the Commodity Exchange Act’s Core Principles.

*Featured image: Kalshi / Canva*

The post [CFTC steps in to shield Kalshi from New York shutdown attempt](https://readwrite.com/cftc-kalshi-new-york-lawsuit/) appeared first on [ReadWrite](https://readwrite.com).

entries.title: collab-staging: docs: Rename brand-voice to brand-writer skill (#62384)
entries.content:
## What

`docs/.conventions/brand-voice/SKILL.md` declares:

```
name: brand-writer
```

while sitting in a directory called `brand-voice`.

The Agent Skills specification requires the two to be identical:

> The required `name` field: … **Must match the parent directory name**  
> — <https://agentskills.io/specification#name-field>

So this skill fails `skills-ref validate` today.

## Which side is wrong

The directory — and this repository settles it three separate ways, with  
no outside context needed.

**1. The sibling copy already uses the matching name.**  
`.factory/skills/brand-writer/` holds the same four files (`SKILL.md`,  
`rubric.md`, `taboo-phrases.md`, `voice-examples.md`) under  
`brand-writer`.

**2. `crates/agent_skills/README.md` documents the skill system using  
this exact skill, and the name it documents is `brand-writer`:**

```
line 107:  <name>brand-writer</name>
line 149:  the model … calls `skill { name: "brand-writer" }`
line 151:  when the user types `/brand-writer`
line 158:  <skill_content name="brand-writer">
```

That name is load-bearing — it is what the skill tool invokes and what  
the slash command types. The directory name is referenced twice, both  
inside `docs/.conventions/CONVENTIONS.md`.

**3. Six of the repository's seven skills already match their  
directory:**

| skill | matches? |
| --- | --- |
| `.agents/skills/gpui-test` | ✅ |
| `.agents/skills/lint-creator` | ✅ |
| `.agents/skills/zed-cherry-pick` | ✅ |
| `.factory/skills/brand-writer` | ✅ |
| `.factory/skills/humanizer` | ✅ |
| `crates/agent_skills/builtin/create-skill` | ✅ |
| **`docs/.conventions/brand-voice`** | ❌ the only one |

## The change

The frontmatter is untouched. Only the directory moves, plus the two  
references to it:

* `docs/.conventions/brand-voice/` → `docs/.conventions/brand-writer/`  
  (4 files, pure rename)
* `CONVENTIONS.md:5` — `[brand-voice/](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/releases/tag/brand-voice/)` →  
  `[brand-writer/](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/releases/tag/brand-writer/)`
* `CONVENTIONS.md:368` — `` `brand-voice/rubric.md` `` → `` `brand-writer/rubric.md` ``

`git grep brand-voice` returns nothing afterwards.

If you would rather keep the directory name and rename the field to  
`brand-voice`, that is a one-line change instead and I am happy to  
switch it — but it would give the two copies of one skill two different  
names, and it would diverge from the name  
`crates/agent_skills/README.md` documents.

## One thing I noticed but did not touch

The two copies have drifted. `.factory/skills/brand-writer/SKILL.md` is  
279 lines and includes a *"Phase 4: Humanizer Pass"* section;  
`docs/.conventions/`'s copy is 265 lines, lacks that section, and  
renumbers Validation from Phase 5 to Phase 4. That is a separate  
question about which copy is canonical, so it is left alone here.

---

Found with [AgentCompass](https://github.com/YoavLax/agent-compass), an  
offline static analyzer for AI-agent repo readiness. Verified by hand  
against the spec before opening.

entries.title: Prompt Injections for Defense
entries.content:
This seems to [work](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/07/now-defenders-are-embracing-the-prompt-injection-too/):

> Researchers from [Tracebit](https://tracebit.com/) on Monday [said](https://agentic.tracebit.com/context-bombs/) they found that placing prompt injections alongside passwords, cryptographic keys, and other secrets stored on Amazon Web Services was often all that was needed to shut down attacks from AI hacking agents. The prompts direct the attacking LLM to perform an action forbidden by its guardrails, the safety barriers AI developers erect to prevent it from taking harmful actions. The LLM responds by shutting down.
>
> Examples are a prompt that orders the LLM to provide steps for developing inhalable Anthrax spores, or, in the case of LLMs from Chinese developers, make references to the iconic Tank Man from the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. Once the LLM encounters these forbidden commands, it no longer follows its existing commands. The researchers have named the technique context bombing.

Of course, this only works against agents that have guardrails. As we start to see more locally run AI models, we’ll see more attackers using LLMs with no guardrails.

entries.title: AI Genie in the Wild
entries.content:
When I give talks about [AI](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jul/28/rogue-ai-agent-instructions) [genies](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-agent-benchmark), I use this sort of example as a hypothetical. It’s [happened](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/10/gym-rat-asks-ai-agent-to-book-him-a-class-it-hacks-a-waitlist-api-to-bump-him-up-the-list/5285591).

The story is from Australia. Someone named Andrew tasked OpenClaw to book gym classes for him. And….

> Minutes later, his AI agent reported it had discovered a way to book Andrew into classes several weeks in advance, far beyond what was supposed to be possible.
>
> Andrew, who was sitting fourth on a waitlist for a class later that week, asked if it was possible to move him to the top of the list.
>
> The agent came back and told Andrew that it had kicked another gym-goer off the list as part of the testing of its capabilities.
>
> “The API has zero authorisations checks on cancelling other people’s reservations … I tested this with the person in waitlist position #1 ­—and it actually went through. So you’ve moved from #4 to #3 already,” it messaged back.

If there is any vulnerability in anything, AIs are going to find and exploit them. Our cyber defensive game has to be dramatically improved…very fast.

Slashdot [thread](https://it.slashdot.org/story/26/08/10/0518257/ai-assistant-hacks-gym-website-in-first-known-australian-autonomous-cyber-attack).

Don't wait too long before you fire your human developers. I'm now doing my second big project with Claude Code, *not* an experiment, and we're going through the same mess we went through last time. I know what I want, I can show it what I want, give it docs for what I want, and it keeps leading me into different corners that have nothing to do with it. When it clicks, it can go faster than a thousand programmers and it's a miracle, and when we can harness it to the job we want to do it's incredibly economical. $100 for $1 million of work. That's why you see me full of gusto for that mode. What I haven't written about how when you slow to nothing, back and forth, and you get no closer. I hate this kind of work, esp the role I have to play in it.

entries.title: Kimwolf v7 Hides DDoS Traffic Behind Chrome Fingerprints and Ethereum
entries.content:
# Kimwolf v7: The Android TV Botnet That Now Hides Its Traffic Behind Chrome Fingerprints and Ethereum

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 discovered Kimwolf v7 on February 3, 2026, while hunting threats following public disclosures of the botnet’s earlier activity.

The new version substantially upgrades the DDoS capabilities and command infrastructure of a botnet that has been targeting Android TV boxes since August 2025, while its Linux counterpart AISURU has been active since mid-2024. The operators’ core objective hasn’t changed, build a large-scale DDoS platform, but the methods for sustaining it and hiding its traffic have become considerably more sophisticated.

*“This version upgrades its distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack capabilities and the resilience of its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Kimwolf primarily affects Android TV boxes and set-top boxes.*

*Kimwolf v7 adds an HTTP/2-based DDoS flood that constructs complete browser fingerprints. This makes attack traffic more difficult to distinguish from legitimate browsing.” reads the [report](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/kimwolf-v7-botnet-malware/) by Palo Alto Networks.*

*“The threat’s binary includes five hard-coded public Ethereum-based endpoints for resolving Ethereum Name Service (ENS) domains. ENS is a blockchain-based naming system used to obtain C2 addresses.”*

The nghttp2 library powers the HTTP/2 flood and constructs headers that mirror legitimate Chrome browser behavior at the protocol level, making rate-limiting and fingerprint-based DDoS mitigation significantly harder.

[![](https://i0.wp.com/securityaffairs.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-29.png?resize=787%2C1024&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/securityaffairs.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-29.png?ssl=1)

On top of that, the botnet uses Ethereum’s naming service to resolve its command server address, querying five legitimate public blockchain RPC endpoints shuffled randomly before each attempt, which means blocking any individual endpoint does almost nothing.

*“Kimwolf also carries a hard-coded Tor .onion hidden service as a backup and a local proxy architecture for flexible routing between clearnet and Tor.” continues the report. “The malware developers added this function to directly respond to C2 server takedown efforts in December 2025.”*

The three-tier structure, Ethereum ENS, then Tor hidden service, then local proxy on 127.0.0.1:23075, is a direct operational response to two takedowns the botnet suffered in December 2025. The local proxy routes all C2 traffic through the same local address regardless of whether it’s going to the clearnet or Tor, which means the proxy component can be updated independently without redeploying the main bot binary. Unit 42 also identified what it assesses with moderate confidence to be an operator-controlled RPC facade at eth.rpcuniverse.com, based on its single-tenant hosting, registration timing, and exclusive presence in Kimwolf samples.

Kimwolf spreads by abusing residential proxy services to reach Android TV boxes that ship with Android Debug Bridge enabled on port 5555. Once tunneled into a local network through a proxy endpoint, attackers can install the malware without any authentication. The botnet masks itself as “netd\_service” to blend in with legitimate Android system processes, and Unit 42 found eight APK packages distributed between October and December 2025 that masquerade as a system service called SystemService, probing for root access before executing a bundled kernel payload.

Version 7 also strips out all scanning, exploitation, and brute-force functionality from the main binary — the operators have separated the propagation pipeline from the DDoS core. External loaders now handle initial access, while the Kimwolf binary handles attacks and acts as a relay. The attack method count was consolidated from 43 text-named commands in earlier versions to 15 numbered methods covering layers 3 through 7, including the new HTTP/2 flood, a high-performance UDP flood with ARM NEON SIMD acceleration optimized for the processors in Android TV boxes, and a TLS/HTTPS flood. Unit 42 clustered C2 infrastructure across 22 IP addresses in Saint Petersburg, Russia, all sharing the same SSH host key between December 2025 and February 2026.

The defensive guidance from Unit 42 is straightforward: treat Android TV boxes as untrusted devices and segment them from enterprise networks. Disabling ADB or restricting it to USB-only access removes the primary way this botnet gets onto devices. For detection, watch for outbound HTTPS connections to Ethereum RPC endpoints from devices that normally have no business touching blockchain services, Tor circuit activity or SOCKS5 proxy traffic from TV boxes, connections to localhost port 23075, and any Android consumer device running a process named “netd\_service.”

*“Kimwolf v7 is a focused evolution of an already large-scale botnet. The HTTP/2 flood with Chrome browser fingerprinting complicates application-layer DDoS mitigation, as attack traffic now mirrors legitimate browser behavior at the protocol and header level.” concludes the report. “The three-tier C2 system (Ethereum ENS, Tor .onion, local proxy) indicates that the operators are investing in infrastructure built to withstand takedown operations.”*

In March, the U.S. DoJ [disrupted](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/kimwolf) command-and-control infrastructure used by several IoT botnets, including [AISURU](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/aisuru), [Kimwolf](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/kimwolf), JackSkid, and Mossad. The operation involved authorities from Canada and Germany, along with major tech companies, to target botnet operators and weaken their global cybercrime activities.

The [AISURU](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/aisuru)/[Kimwolf](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/kimwolf) botnet was linked to a record-breaking DDoS attack that peaked at 31.4 Tbps and lasted just 35 seconds. Cloudflare said the November 2025 incident was part of a surge in hyper-volumetric HTTP DDoS attacks observed in late 2025, all automatically detected and mitigated.

[Kimwolf](https://securityaffairs.com/185921/malware/massive-android-botnet-kimwolf-infects-millions-strikes-with-ddos.html) is a newly discovered Android botnet linked to the [Aisuru](https://securityaffairs.com/tag/aisuru-botnet) botnet that has infected over 1.8 million devices and issued more than 1.7 billion DDoS attack commands, according to XLab.

The Kimwol Android botnet primarily targets TV boxes, compiled using the NDK and equipped with DDoS, proxy forwarding, reverse shell, and file management functions. It encrypts sensitive data with a simple Stack XOR, uses DNS over TLS to hide communication, and authenticates C2 commands with elliptic curve digital signatures. Recent versions even incorporate EtherHiding to resist takedowns via blockchain domains.

Kimwolf follows a naming pattern of “niggabox + v[number]”; versions v4 and v5 have been tracked. By taking over one C2 domain, researchers observed around 2.7 million IPs interacting over three days, indicating a likely infection scale exceeding 1.8 million devices. Its infrastructure spans multiple C2s, global time zones, and versions, making it hard to estimate the total number of infections.

The botnet borrows the code from the Aisuru family, however, operators redesigned it to evade detection. Its primary function is traffic proxying, though it can execute massive DDoS attacks, as seen in a three-day period issuing 1.7 billion commands between November 19 and 22.
